title: Documentation reads comfortably on every screen, with framed code blocks
audience: People reading Stackweaver documentation, blog articles and module READMEs in the frontend.
before: Guide text ran the full width of the content column, so lines grew very long on wide screens. Code blocks had a transparent body, tables drew a line between every column, and the selected page in the docs sidebar used a flat grey.
after: Guide text sits in a centred column that widens with the space available, from about 74 characters per line on a laptop to about 120 on a wide display, and code blocks, tables and diagrams grow beyond it when their content needs the room. Code blocks have a framed look with a tinted title bar, and blocks without a language show window dots. Tables use row lines and a tinted header, and the selected sidebar page and the search box use the same faint tint.
action: Update the frontend image. No configuration change is required.
details: Collapsing or narrowing a docs sidebar pane gives the text longer lines.
Code inside a numbered step stays at the step's width and scrolls when a line is longer.

title: The homepage answers common Stackweaver questions
audience: People evaluating Stackweaver for their team.
before: Setup, compatibility, licensing and help were described on separate pages.
after: The homepage groups five answers with links to setup guides, compatibility details, the license and consultancy.
action: Open Frequently asked questions on the homepage.
details: Use a mouse, touch or keyboard to expand an answer.

title: Homepage install cards follow the setup guides
audience: Anyone choosing a self-hosted installation from the homepage.
before: The short examples missed required setup, and guide links could leave a prefixed installation.
after: The cards point to their prerequisites, show a pinned Helm install or a Kustomize render, and open guides within the configured public path.
action: Follow the guide for your deployment method before running the example.
details: The Compose command assumes the bundle has been configured. The Kustomize command renders a file for review.

title: Blog articles stay readable while the page loads
audience: Readers opening the blog index or a published article, including comparisons.
before: The page could briefly replace visible text with a loading screen while its interactive controls downloaded.
after: The text stays visible while the interactive page downloads.
action: Update the frontend image. No configuration change is required.

title: The Ansible product page loads only the visible screenshot
audience: People browsing the public Ansible page.
before: The page requested both light and dark screenshots as soon as it opened.
after: With JavaScript enabled, the browser loads the visible screenshot near the viewport and requests the other image when the reader switches themes.
action: Update the frontend image. No configuration change is required.
details: The page reserves space for the screenshot while it loads.

title: Documentation stays stable while a guide loads
audience: People opening documentation in the frontend.
before: Document navigation and the footer could briefly appear in the visible loading area, then move when the guide arrived.
after: The loading placeholder reserves at least one viewport of space, keeping navigation and the footer below the initial viewport until content is available.
action: Update the frontend image. No configuration change is required.
details: Loaded guides keep their existing layout and shared code presentation.

title: Documentation loads indexed source files directly
audience: People browsing documentation in the frontend.
before: Leaf articles requested two missing folder README files before loading their actual Markdown source.
after: The viewer first requests a source listed in its generated collection index. Folder precedence, relative links and legacy fallbacks for stale or unavailable indexes are preserved.
action: Update the frontend image. No configuration change is required.
details: Relative links retain their document or directory context.
HTML fallback responses are rejected rather than rendered as Markdown.

title: Jobs warn when inventory refresh did not succeed
audience: Anyone launching jobs against inventory with update-on-launch sources.
before: A job could continue after a failed pre-launch inventory refresh without clearly telling you that its hosts came from an earlier sync.
after: The job still runs against the last successfully synced hosts, with a warning above its tabs and at the start of its output. A refresh still running after 30 minutes also stops holding the job and produces a warning. If the source has never synced successfully, the job runs without hosts from that source.
action: Check the warning before relying on the result. Correct the source error and sync again if the job needs current inventory. A warning does not mean that the job itself failed.
details: Each warning identifies the source and reason, with the last successful sync time when one exists. A timeout warning means the sync has not finished; it does not mean the sync completed with an error.
The warning is available with platform and self-hosted runners, including ad hoc commands and launches from schedules and workflows.
API clients receive inventory-sync-warnings on the job. Existing template notifications include warnings and extra.inventory_sync_warnings; no additional notification trigger is required.

title: Failed inventory syncs preserve the last successful inventory
audience: Operators of dynamic inventory sources, especially sources with overwrite enabled.
before: An authentication, connectivity or configuration failure could be recorded as a successful sync with no hosts. With overwrite enabled, that result could remove every host and group owned by the source.
after: These failures are recorded as failed syncs. The output includes the plugin error, and the last successful hosts and groups remain available.
action: If a sync fails, fix the reported error and retry it. A successful sync that genuinely finds no hosts can still remove source-owned rows when overwrite is enabled.
details: The preservation rule also applies to a constructed inventory build that cannot parse an input or its rules. It keeps the last successful hosts, groups and memberships.
A failed refresh and a successful empty result are different outcomes. Overwrite continues to prune rows after a successful sync; it is not disabled by this fix.

title: Constructed inventories accept derived hosts and groups only
audience: Anyone who added hosts or groups by hand, through the API or through Terraform to a constructed inventory.
before: Hand-created rows could coexist with derived inventory even though a rebuild replaces the materialized set. Earlier rebuilds could also leave stale hosts and empty groups behind.
after: Hosts and groups come from the inputs and rules. Writes that create a host, group or source, add group membership, or move a group under another are refused with 409 Conflict. The next successful rebuild removes stale rows, including manually added rows that are not derived.
action: Before upgrading, move any manually added host or group you still need into an input inventory, or derive it with a rule. Terraform host and group resources targeting a constructed inventory receive the same refusal.
details: Reading inventory, disabling a host, and deleting hosts, groups or memberships remain available. Other inventory types are unaffected.
A parsing failure preserves the last successful build. Removal of stale rows happens after a successful rebuild.
Recording sync status no longer writes removed inventory rows back or overwrites unrelated inventory edits made while the sync runs.

title: Explore the API through one generated reference
audience: People integrating Stackweaver with automation and API clients.
before: Separate endpoint catalogues could disagree about available operations and request fields.
after: The API explorer presents the generated operation descriptions, parameters and response examples in one place.
action: Use the API explorer to inspect operations. Follow Using the API for authentication context, pagination and retrieving a deployment-specific description.
details: The narrative integration guide links to the operation reference rather than maintaining another endpoint catalogue.

title: Browse documentation from a generated homepage
audience: Readers of Stackweaver documentation.
before: Finding a starting guide meant following individual article links.
after: The documentation homepage groups sections with descriptions and a prominent search. Its destinations come from the generated documentation index.
action: No configuration change is required. Use the documentation navigation to find the relevant guide.
details: Existing article links remain available.

title: Read product changes and upgrade actions in one changelog
audience: Readers of Stackweaver documentation.
before: Feature-specific notes and component release pages were separate starting points for understanding changes.
after: The central changelog explains affected users, upgrade actions and confirmed availability for each required component.
action: Read the action for each relevant change and compare its component release links with your installation. The listed versions are confirmation evidence, not a minimum supported bundle.
details: Only reviewed entries with complete component evidence appear in the feed. Earlier notes remain available during the separate history review.

title: Clearer guides with maintained visuals and generated references
audience: Readers and operators using the public Stackweaver documentation.
before: Public guides mixed task instructions with implementation history and repeated reference lists, while screenshots had no shared freshness check.
after: Reviewed guides provide visible configuration examples, maintained product screenshots and focused diagrams. A generated capability catalogue and central changelog keep repeated facts in their source pipelines.
action: Use the current task guides and canonical references. No deployment configuration change is required for this documentation update.
details: The original Ansible changelog remains available while its migration is reviewed.
Documentation images use the active light or dark theme when expanded, and optional background uses the shared disclosure styling.
Security guides distinguish verified release evidence from compliance claims, and linked live Scorecard badges remain available in both themes.

title: Browser sign-in uses a server-side session
audience: Browser users and operators upgrading Stackweaver.
before: Browser authentication depended on OAuth tokens held by the SPA.
after: The API signs in as a confidential Zitadel client and gives the browser an opaque HttpOnly session cookie. The SPA holds no OAuth token.
action: Create the confidential BFF application and provide its credentials before an external-Zitadel upgrade. Preserve HTTPS, the app URL and cookie/CSRF headers. Sign in again after upgrading; replace Zitadel bearer tokens in scripts with tfe- API tokens.
details: Default session limits are one hour idle, twelve hours absolute and a five-minute identity liveness check. Unknown identity liveness retries after 30 seconds; idle and absolute expiry remain effective.
Required sign-in factors must be verified before completing login. Existing browser sessions do not resynchronize SSO groups; changes apply at the next sign-in.

Bundled initializers reconcile a one-hour Zitadel access-token lifetime for other applications. Configure a different lifetime explicitly when required; that lifetime does not control BFF browser-session duration.
Scripts, Terraform CLI and runners use their programmatic credentials rather than browser-session cookies. Use tfe- API tokens where an API token is required.

title: Encrypt saved plans when encryption at rest is configured
audience: Operators of the platform queue-mode OpenTofu runner.
before: Saved plan files could be stored without application-level encryption between plan and apply.
after: The platform runner seals saved plans using the configured encryption service and reads legacy plaintext plans.
action: Upgrade participating platform runners together: older runners cannot read newly encrypted plans. Keep the same encryption key across those runners before applying outstanding plans.
details: An older runner cannot consume newly encrypted plan files. With no encryption service configured, plan storage remains plaintext.
This change concerns the platform queue-mode runner; it does not change the self-hosted agent execution path.

title: Separate install-wide administration from organization ownership
audience: Installation administrators and automation managing the OpenTofu version catalogue.
before: Install-wide operations did not have the current explicit platform-administrator boundary.
after: Platform administrators manage installation-wide resources without receiving organization membership. Organization owners do not receive platform privileges.
action: Declare installation administrators, especially with external Zitadel. Mint a personal token explicitly carrying platform:admin for install-wide provider automation; plain CLI, organization and team tokens do not grant it.
details: The bundled bootstrap administrator is the fallback when the declared administrator list is empty. External identity installations must declare their administrators.
Organization default OpenTofu versions are configured in organization settings. Organization creation remains open to signed-in users unless the installation restricts it to platform administrators.

title: Require explicit registration scopes and confirmed runner bindings
audience: Operators registering self-hosted runners or reading agent-pool queue depth.
before: General-purpose registration credentials and failed binding lookups could be treated too broadly.
after: Registration requires an explicit runner registration scope. Failed or mismatched binding checks refuse the request.
action: Use an explicitly scoped runner-registration credential or a pool-bound agent token. Replace unscoped or wildcard general-purpose registration keys.
details: Registration requires org:<organization-id>:runner:register. A mismatched pool or organization is refused; an unreadable pool binding is a server error rather than unrestricted access.
An intentionally unbound but correctly scoped registration credential can still name a pool in its organization.

title: Keep the verified email while a new address awaits verification
audience: People changing their account email address.
before: A profile edit could replace the stored email before the new address was verified.
after: The account retains its verified address while the proposed address is reported as unconfirmed-email. Verified sign-in synchronizes the new address.
action: Complete verification through the configured identity service and sign in with the verified account. A deployment without the profile service refuses a changed email.
details: Resubmitting the same address, ignoring case, does not trigger another verification request.

title: Reject unsupported VCS providers when creating connections
audience: People or automation creating VCS connections.
before: Placeholder provider connections could be accepted and then fail when used.
after: Connection creation accepts the implemented github and azure_devops providers and rejects unsupported values immediately.
action: Use GitHub or Azure DevOps for a new connection. Review existing placeholder connections; this change does not migrate or delete them.

title: Configure Ansible repository access through VCS connections
audience: People configuring repository access for Ansible automation.
before: The API and UI exposed SCM/VCS credential options that execution did not consume.
after: The unsupported scm API credential type and the unused vcs UI option are removed from creation. Existing stored credentials are not migrated or deleted.
action: Configure repository access through a VCS connection instead of creating an Ansible SCM credential.
details: Existing stored credential rows are not migrated or deleted by this change. Supported machine, vault and cloud credentials retain their own execution roles.

guides.title: Register Ansible playbooks and repository access

title: Load public pages independently of application screens
audience: People opening the landing page, documentation, sign-in and application screens.
before: Opening the landing page loaded unrelated application screens and an oversized default logo before the visitor could use the page.
after: Public pages open without downloading unrelated application screens. Navigation shows loading feedback and offers a reload action if the requested page cannot be downloaded.
action: No configuration changes are required. Reload an open page if a page update leaves an unavailable code chunk.
details: Existing links, browser sessions, themes and landing-page layouts are preserved. Application navigation shows loading feedback and offers an explicit reload if a page cannot be downloaded.
The landing tour defers inactive screenshots and keeps its last loaded image visible during a transition. Backend request latency is unchanged.

title: Find guides through generated documentation overviews
audience: Readers finding setup instructions and task guides in the documentation.
before: Section overviews used manually maintained directory lists or tables, and the documentation root presented uniformly sized folder cards.
after: The main overview highlights the first section. Section pages combine folder cards and article links, while keeping their setup guidance and capability references.
action: No configuration changes are required. Existing guide URLs remain available.
details: The existing viewer header, folder sidebar and article frame are preserved.
External Markdown links keep their original destination, and relative Markdown links with fragments resolve to the intended document heading.
Generated folder navigation stays in step with available documentation. Explanatory articles retain their authored content.

title: Show distinct documentation commands correctly
audience: Readers using code examples in documentation and other shared Markdown views.
before: Code blocks in the same language that shared their first 100 characters could display the same highlighted snippet, even when their remaining commands differed.
after: The highlighting cache uses the complete code block, so examples with a shared prefix retain their distinct displayed content.
action: Reload an open documentation page after updating the frontend. No configuration change is required.
details: Copy uses the block source. Displayed examples and copied text are checked together by the regression.
This corrects ordinary fenced code blocks; it does not redesign CodeGroup navigation.

title: Read verified component changes in the central changelog
audience: Operators checking changes and upgrade actions for their installation.
before: An unavailable release-provenance asset in one component prevented the evidence refresh from retaining verified observations for other components.
after: Verified component observations are retained independently. Entries still require evidence for every component they need, and incomplete entries stay out of the public feed.
action: Read the action and confirmed component versions for relevant entries before upgrading. No deployment setting is changed by the changelog refresh.
details: Each entry leads with its user impact. Previous behavior and supporting scope remain available in expandable details.

title: Prepare frequently visited application screens after the dashboard loads
audience: People navigating from the dashboard into Workspaces, Playbooks and Job Templates.
before: The first visit to each application screen downloaded its page code during navigation.
after: After the signed-in dashboard finishes its initial requests, up to three frequently used screens prepare their code in the background. Hovering, focusing or pressing navigation links also prepares their destination.
action: No configuration changes are required. Use the existing reload action if a page download fails.
details: Background preparation loads code only. Resource data is requested when its screen opens, so backend response time still affects content readiness.
Idle preparation pauses for hidden tabs, offline browsers and restricted connections. Landing-page route isolation and existing navigation controls are preserved.

title: Collect release history from verified registry provenance
audience: Contributors refreshing the central changelog.
before: Releases without an attached provenance file could not establish availability even when they published valid GitHub artifact attestations.
after: The read-only refresh can verify published OCI provenance with the exact release identity when the GitHub Release has no provenance attachment.
action: Use the current GitHub CLI and review the refreshed evidence snapshot before publication. No running-deployment change is required.
details: The artifact digest, tag commit, source sync and successful release run must agree.
An invalid attachment or failed cryptographic verification still fails closed.

title: Session list no longer shows a placeholder expiry date
audience: People reviewing their signed-in sessions under Settings > Sessions.
before: A session without an expiration showed "Expires: 1/1/1".
after: A session without an expiration shows no expiry line, and the API leaves out its expiration-date attribute.
action: No action is required.

title: The initializer repairs the address of SSO group webhooks
audience: Operators syncing SSO groups to teams through Zitadel Actions.
before: Rerunning the initializer kept an existing Actions target at the address it was first registered with, so a corrected ACTIONS_API_BASE_URL did not reach Zitadel.
after: When ACTIONS_API_BASE_URL is set, each initializer run moves the idp-sync and complement-token targets to that address and keeps their signing keys. Without it, existing targets keep their address.
action: If SSO groups do not reach Stackweaver, set ACTIONS_API_BASE_URL to the API address Zitadel can reach and run the initializer again.

title: Public pages and configurable search indexing
audience: People evaluating Stackweaver and operators publishing its public pages.
before: Public routes depended on the browser application shell, and missing crawler files could return successful HTML.
after: Public product pages and documentation have initial HTML, page metadata and canonical URLs. A shared catalogue generates the sitemap; private application routes retain the application shell and noindex policy. Unknown public pages and missing assets return 404.
action: Search indexing is opt-in. Configure the installation HTTPS URL and enable public indexing when you intend to publish it. Helm uses frontend.publicSite.url and frontend.publicSite.indexing; the Compose guide provides an optional nginx settings override. Review callbacks and trusted origins separately when changing the app hostname.
details: Self-hosted deployments retain their own domain. An unconfigured installation requests noindex and does not expose a sitemap.
Only published articles enter the production blog and sitemap. Draft comparisons remain excluded.
Documentation and articles use the same code-block presentation; deployment and static-render adapters stay separate from application services.

title: Featured stories in the blog archive
audience: Readers and maintainers of the public Stackweaver blog.
before: The first source-file entry always occupied the lead card, and every article cover used a comparison label.
after: Published stories can be featured explicitly, topic filters follow available articles, and vision articles have their own cover and banner wording.
action: No action is required for existing articles. Authors may set featured: true in article metadata; draft articles remain excluded from production.
details: Editorial manuscripts and present-tense launch copy remain drafts until separately published.

title: Infrastructure automation articles in the public blog
audience: Visitors evaluating Stackweaver and maintainers publishing its public frontend.
before: The production blog excluded the editorial manuscripts as drafts.
after: Five approved articles are included in public initial HTML, blog discovery, article metadata and the sitemap when indexing is enabled. They cover AAP, Semaphore UI, Terraform Cloud alternatives, the founder vision and AI-agent workflows.
action: Deploy the updated frontend to serve the articles. Preserve the deployment-specific public origin and indexing settings; source publication does not configure DNS or change a private installation's default noindex policy.
details: Articles use maintained product images, theme-paired editorial artwork and distinct author pull quotes.
The owner approved the launch-day product copy for publication; this content update does not itself release additional product interfaces.

title: Consistent Blog navigation on mobile
audience: Readers using the public website on phones and tablets.
before: The mobile Blog link was misaligned, and Docs stayed highlighted while reading the blog.
after: Blog and Docs use matching spacing and typography. The current section is highlighted and identified to assistive technology, and selecting either link closes the mobile menu.
action: Deploy the updated frontend. No configuration change is required.

title: A first Docker Compose install survives an interrupted initializer
audience: Operators installing Stackweaver with Docker Compose.
before: The initializer wrote its generated client secrets and login token to .env only at the end of a successful run, so a run that stopped part-way lost values Zitadel returns only once, and a first install whose back-channel logout or Actions address named the API failed, because Zitadel cannot save an address on a host that is not running yet.
after: The initializer records each generated value in .env the moment Zitadel returns it, replacing the file atomically, so the next run recovers a run that stopped part-way. While the API's host does not resolve, it creates the sign-in app without the back-channel logout URI and the Actions targets at a holding address on Zitadel, and its api-urls run (ZITADEL_INIT_MODE=api-urls), or its next full run, registers the API's addresses once the API is up.
action: No action is required. To register the back-channel logout URI and Actions targets on a first install, run the initializer with ZITADEL_INIT_MODE=api-urls after the API is healthy, or run the initializer again.
details: ZITADEL_INIT_ENV_FILE names another path for the generated values; the default is deploy/.env under the initializer's PROJECT_ROOT.
Because .env is replaced rather than rewritten in place, a container that bind-mounts .env as a single file sees the version that existed when it started.

title: Ansible deletes succeed for jobs that used credentials
audience: Ansible users who delete job templates, playbooks, inventories, projects or organizations, and operators who set a job retention period.
before: Deleting a job template failed with a database error when any of its jobs had run with a credential. A force delete of a playbook or inventory, a project or organization delete, and the scheduled removal of expired jobs failed the same way when the jobs they reached had used credentials.
after: These deletes remove each job together with the record of the credentials it ran with, and complete. The credentials themselves are kept.
action: Deploy the updated API. No configuration change is required.
details: A credential that a remaining job ran with cannot be deleted on its own. The 409 response names those jobs as the reason. It no longer lists job templates and inventory sources, which do not block the delete.

When a job template or job starts using an inventory, or a job template starts using a playbook, while that inventory or playbook is being deleted, the 409 response names that template or job and how to remove it. It no longer lists inventory sources for an inventory or jobs for a playbook at that point, because those do not block the database delete.

title: Cookie preferences match the current design
audience: Visitors choosing cookie preferences on the public website.
before: The cookie banner used older styling, small controls and custom toggles without accessible names.
after: The banner and preferences panel use the current shared design, named keyboard-accessible switches and larger action controls. The category list scrolls on short screens while the actions remain visible.
action: Deploy the updated frontend. Existing saved consent choices are preserved; no configuration change is required.

title: Deleting a playbook keeps the history of its jobs
audience: Ansible users who delete playbook registrations, and API clients that read jobs.
before: A playbook that any job had run could not be deleted. The delete answered 409 until those jobs were removed, which meant giving up their logs, results and events. A force delete removed every job that had run the playbook.
after: A playbook delete is blocked only by job templates that use the playbook and by jobs using it that are still pending or running. Jobs that ran the playbook keep their logs, results and events, and the job page shows the playbook by the name it had when the job ran, marked as deleted and without a link. A force delete cancels the jobs that have not finished, removes the jobs of the job templates it deletes and keeps the jobs that ran the playbook directly. The playbook's cached snapshot and stored content are removed from object storage.
action: Deploy the updated API, frontend and Ansible runner, including self-hosted Ansible agents. No configuration change is required. Existing jobs take their playbook's current name the first time the updated API starts.
details: A job's playbook-name attribute holds the name of the playbook it ran, recorded at launch. It stays after the playbook is deleted, when the job no longer has a playbook relationship. It is empty for ad hoc jobs.
A job whose playbook was deleted cannot be relaunched. The relaunch answers 409 and the job page disables Relaunch.
Platform runners and self-hosted agents stop a running job that is deleted, for example with its job template, as they stop a canceled one.

title: Deleting a project or organization removes its stored objects
audience: Anyone who deletes workspaces, projects or organizations, and operators who manage the object storage bucket.
before: Deleting a project or organization removed its rows and left its objects in storage: state files, run logs, saved plans, configuration uploads and playbook content, and for an organization its registry modules and providers. Deleting a workspace removed its state and run objects and left its configuration uploads.
after: A workspace, project or organization delete removes the objects of everything it deleted once the delete has committed. Objects that other workspaces, projects or organizations still use are kept. If storage cannot be reached the delete still succeeds, the failure is logged, and those objects stay.
action: Deploy the updated API. No configuration change is required. Objects left by deletes made before this version stay in storage.
details: Deleting a project keeps the organization's registry modules and providers, which belong to the organization.
An organization's registry objects are removed by the paths its versions recorded, so versions published before the organization was renamed are included.

title: Public pages have clearer navigation and smaller logo downloads
audience: Visitors reading Stackweaver public pages and installation guides.
before: A generic privacy link, outdated API-reference links and a low-contrast blog callout made parts of public navigation less clear. Compact navigation logos used the larger hero image.
after: The privacy link describes its destination, guides open the current API explorer and credential section, the blog callout has readable colors in both themes, and navigation selects a smaller version of the same logo artwork.
action: Update the frontend image to receive these changes. Existing consent choices and supported deployment configuration are preserved.
details: Navigation image variants are selected for the rendered size and pixel density; the hero artwork remains available at its existing resolution.

title: Public pages link Ansible evaluation and a tested walkthrough
audience: Visitors evaluating Ansible automation and reading the public blog.
before: Blog visits loaded homepage presentation code and the archive included full article bodies. The Ansible page did not link its relevant comparisons or a practical walkthrough.
after: Public pages preload their own route, the blog archive loads article summaries, and contextual links lead from the homepage to Ansible comparisons and a tested manual-run and scheduling walkthrough.
action: Update the frontend image to receive the public pages and navigation changes. No configuration change is required.

title: Inline code keeps documentation articles stable
audience: Readers of documentation containing inline code.
before: Inline code triggered asynchronous block highlighting, replacing the article after its first render and losing selection or keyboard focus.
after: Inline code renders directly. Articles without asynchronously highlighted fenced blocks keep their existing content and keyboard focus.
action: No action is required.
details: Fenced code continues to highlight asynchronously and retains its language labels and copy controls.

title: Formatted documentation headings have anchors in initial HTML
audience: Readers following section links in public documentation or articles.
before: Headings with inline code, emphasis or links had empty anchor IDs in initial HTML. The documentation table of contents repaired them after JavaScript ran.
after: Heading anchors include their complete visible text in initial HTML and browser rendering. Existing plain-text heading anchors are preserved.
action: Update the frontend image. No configuration or documentation-link change is required.

title: Repository pickers select their sole connection after returning
audience: People browsing playbook repositories with one VCS connection.
before: Returning to a repository picker while its connection list was cached could leave the connection unselected and hide the repository selector.
after: A sole connection is selected from cached or newly loaded data. Deliberate connection choices and clears survive refresh, and repository or branch drafts stay with their original connection.
action: No action is required.
details: With multiple connections, choose the connection to browse.

title: Public links include branded previews and a reachable licence reference
audience: Readers sharing links to public pages and operators hosting Stackweaver on their own domain.
before: Public HTML included preview text without a preview image.
after: Public pages provide the existing Stackweaver logo, image dimensions and descriptive alternative text in Open Graph and Twitter metadata. Image URLs use the configured public origin and base path, including after navigation. The three comparison articles link to the public canonical licence, which anonymous visitors can read.
action: Update the frontend image. Preview services control when they refresh cached links.

title: Registry follows the organization in the current route
audience: People browsing private modules and switching organizations.
before: A cached organization list could leave the Registry landing route waiting for a selection, or show the previous organization after switching back.
after: The Registry landing route selects the first available organization from cached or newly loaded data. Organization routes show modules for the organization named in the URL.
action: No action is required.

title: Article recommendations follow the subject and support links are public
audience: Readers exploring Stackweaver articles and troubleshooting guidance.
before: Continue reading links followed source-file order, including unrelated comparisons. The troubleshooting guide linked to an issue tracker anonymous visitors could not access.
after: Continue reading selects up to two other published articles by their main subject and shared subjects, with featured and recent articles as fallbacks. The troubleshooting guide links to the public support policy for choosing a component issue tracker.
action: Update the frontend image. No configuration change is required.
details: Recommendations are present in initial HTML and after browser navigation. Drafts and the current article are excluded.

title: Registry modules fit phone screens
audience: People browsing Registry modules on phones and tablets.
before: The filters and module cards shared a horizontal row at narrow widths, pushing module details outside the visible area.
after: Filters stack above modules on narrow screens. Module names, descriptions and metadata wrap inside their cards, while desktop keeps filters beside modules.
action: No action is required.

title: Module details show version metadata after returning
audience: People browsing private modules in the Registry.
before: Returning to a recently opened module could show a version in the selector while its inputs, outputs and README were missing. An empty module could return to Inputs instead of Versions.
after: Module pages show the first version's metadata when opened from cached or freshly loaded data. Modules without versions open on Versions.
action: Update the frontend. No configuration change is required.
details: Version choices and tabs remain stable on nonempty refreshes. Uploading or deleting a version resets the selection from the refreshed result.

title: Module controls fit phone screens
audience: People reading Registry modules on phones and tablets.
before: Module metadata, tabs and the usage sidebar extended beyond the visible area on narrow screens.
after: Module metadata and tabs wrap within the page on phones and tablets, and usage instructions sit below the main content. Desktop keeps its right sidebar.
action: Update the frontend. No configuration change is required.
details: Tabs, the version selector and sidebar actions are at least 44 pixels high on narrow screens. Long usage lines scroll inside their code block.

title: Published module inputs preserve empty arrays and tuple types
audience: Operators publishing private Registry modules.
before: Empty list, set and tuple defaults appeared as null, and tuple type constraints could repeat the tuple constructor.
after: New module versions preserve empty list, set and tuple defaults as arrays and show tuple type constraints with the intended nesting.
action: Update the API and publish a new module version to regenerate affected metadata. Existing stored versions keep their current metadata.
details: Explicit null defaults remain null. Populated defaults and required-input handling are preserved.

title: Published modules list declared provider requirements
audience: Operators publishing private Registry modules.
before: Provider requirements declared in modern required_providers blocks were missing from published module metadata.
after: New module versions include the provider names, sources and version constraints declared in required_providers blocks.
action: Update the API and publish a new module version to regenerate affected metadata. Existing stored versions keep their current metadata.
details: Legacy attribute-form requirements and default provider sources are preserved.
Provider requirements are read from versions.tf; terraform.tf is used only when versions.tf is absent.

title: Abandoned sign-ins no longer leave Zitadel sessions behind
audience: Operators and people reviewing their sessions under Settings > Sessions.
before: Zitadel sessions created during sign-in had no expiry, so a sign-in that was abandoned or failed stayed in Zitadel indefinitely, including sessions that had passed a password check.
after: Every Zitadel session Stackweaver creates or updates during sign-in expires 15 minutes after the browser-session absolute limit (12 hours 15 minutes by default), counted from its last sign-in step.
action: No action is required. Zitadel sessions created before this release keep no expiry; end them in Zitadel or under Settings > Sessions if you want them gone.

title: Launchers replace the queue runners and agent mode
audience: Everyone who runs OpenTofu runs or Ansible jobs, self-hosted agent pool operators, and operators who install Stackweaver with Helm or Docker Compose.
before: Platform runners took work from a Redis queue and held the database, object storage and Redis credentials, self-hosted agents ran a separate agent mode, and the Helm chart kept runner and Galaxy cache volumes.
after: Every run, job and sync runs through a launcher that claims it from the API and places an executor with a token for that job alone: in its own process, in a container, or in a Kubernetes pod. Launchers hold no database, storage or Redis credential. Hosted capacity, agent pools, run images and execution environments, identity bindings, registry pull Secrets and the organization's verified cache work the same way on every driver.
action: Back up PostgreSQL and the object storage before upgrading, because the upgrade is forward-only and rolling back is a restore. On Helm, remove the runner and Galaxy cache values the upgrade guide lists and set the launcher network ranges before helm upgrade. On Docker Compose, replace docker-compose.yml with the new release's file, which replaces the runner services with launchers. Upgrade self-hosted agents to the launcher image. The API and the orchestrator must share ENCRYPTION_KEY: existing plan JSON is encrypted in the background at the first API start. Job pods use scheduling gates, which need Kubernetes 1.27 or later. If an Ansible job uses a workload identity, update its cloud trust to the job's new subject: a template job and its relaunches use the template's name and an ad hoc command uses adhoc-<module>. Rename any organization, project, workspace, template or job whose name contains a colon, because a run or job with a configured identity now fails when that identity cannot be minted.
details: A lost launcher's running plan or sync is offered again, while a lost apply or Ansible job ends for a person to re-queue, so an apply never runs twice.
A job launched from a template without a pool runs on the project's or organization's agent-mode default pool, as its effective settings show.
Private registry modules install in jobs with a token the job receives for the registry host, and git sources in requirements.yml are cached by the commit their branch or tag resolves to.

Jobs on the container and Kubernetes drivers never reach Azure's platform address 168.63.129.16, in any network mode, and on rootful Podman the jobs network is firewalled through nftables, so the firewall image needs nft.

Ansible jobs receive the Azure, AWS, GCP and Vault per-run identities, under a subject that stays the same across launches, and any run or job fails with the reason when an identity its organization configured cannot be minted.

title: Documentation keeps open sections and keyboard focus
audience: Readers of documentation and articles containing highlighted code.
before: Completing code highlighting, showing copy feedback or changing theme could replace the document and reset open sections or keyboard focus.
after: Code blocks update without replacing the surrounding document. Open sections and keyboard focus survive those updates.
action: No action is required.
details: Existing code-block styling, language labels, copy text and theme-aware highlighting are preserved.
Code blocks keep their shared frame and copy button while highlighting refreshes.

title: Cancelling an apply keeps the state it saved
audience: Anyone who cancels an OpenTofu run while it applies.
before: Cancelling a run during its apply interrupted OpenTofu, but the platform refused the state it saved on interrupt and the final log. Resources the apply had already created, changed or destroyed were missing from the workspace's state, and the log ended without saying the run was canceled.
after: The state OpenTofu saves when an apply is cancelled becomes the workspace's current state version, the apply log keeps OpenTofu's interrupt output and ends with a cancel marker, and the run stays canceled.
action: Deploy the updated API. No configuration change is required. For a run cancelled during its apply before this version, check the workspace against the real resources before the next run.
details: Only the cancelled attempt's final state, log and completion are accepted; every other request for that run is still refused.
A canceled Ansible job keeps its last output and its log ends with a cancel marker, in the same way.

title: Cloud inventory files stay out of playbook choices
audience: Users selecting repository files while registering playbooks or choosing a job template source.
before: Cloud inventory configurations with names such as prod-aws_ec2.yml, prod_azure_rm.yaml or prodgcp_compute.yml could also appear as playbook candidates.
after: The existing aws_ec2, azure_rm and gcp_compute filename suffixes identify cloud inventory configurations with any prefix, while inventory file choices remain available.
action: Update the API and reload the repository file list. Existing registrations are unchanged; review any inventory configurations previously registered as playbooks.
details: Bare and dot-prefixed names, repository directory filters, supported extensions and ordinary YAML file choices retain their existing behavior.
This affects repository discovery only. It does not run inventories, change plugin versions or add other filename aliases.

title: Short playbook import lists stay selectable
audience: Users selecting playbooks to import on a phone or short viewport.
before: A list containing at most three files could collapse inside the import dialog, preventing individual file selection.
after: Short lists retain their row height so each file remains selectable. Longer lists keep their existing scrolling behavior.
action: No action is required.
details: Directory filters and registered-file selection behavior are preserved.

title: Code stays in place while syntax colors load
audience: Readers of guides and articles with code examples.
before: Opening a guide could load syntax highlighting for code well below the viewport, and code blocks changed height when colors appeared.
after: Ordinary code fences request highlighting as you approach them and keep their size and scroll position when colors appear. You can read and copy plain code while the colors load.
action: Update the frontend. No configuration change is required.

title: Public guides stay readable during startup
audience: Readers opening public documentation directly, including on slow connections and customer domains.
before: The browser replaced the generated article with a loading view while downloading its route code and fetching the documentation index and Markdown again.
after: The matching public guide starts from the data included with its HTML and waits for its route code before mounting the interactive viewer.
action: Update the frontend. No configuration change is required.
details: Only the current public documentation page warms its matching cache. Other routes, redirect resolution and customer base paths retain their existing behavior.
Failed route imports retain the reload action; older pages without startup data retain normal source loading.

title: Run pages show platform errors and stop polling finished runs
audience: Everyone who reads OpenTofu run pages.
before: A run that failed before OpenTofu ran, such as a job that could not be placed, showed "Unable to parse error details". A finished plan-only run kept requesting its placement every three seconds, and a run whose apply saved no state logged a client error.
after: The run page shows the platform's error message as reported. Placement polling stops once a run has finished, plan-only runs included, and a run without state outputs takes its outputs from the apply log without an error.
action: No action is required.

title: Run, pool and identity settings are checked when they are saved
audience: Organization owners, agent pool administrators and Terraform provider users who configure run defaults, agent pools and identity bindings.
before: Several settings were accepted on save and failed only when a job used them: CPU and memory limits in any form, an identity binding of another pool, identity bindings without their mechanism's annotation, negative or unbounded run timeouts, and an organization cache limit of any size. A pool named after the hosted pool failed with a server error.
after: Each is refused with 422 on save, with the reason: CPU and memory limits in the forms both drivers read, an identity binding only from the pool the workspace or job template runs on, a binding name of letters, digits, '.', '_' and '-' with its mechanism's required annotation, and run timeouts of zero to 24 hours. An organization owner sets the cache limit up to the deployment's limit, and only a platform administrator above it. A duplicate pool name answers 409.
action: No action is required for existing values; they are checked again only when changed.
details: The identity binding pickers offer only the bindings of the pool the object chooses, and the forms name a negative or over-long timeout and a malformed annotation line instead of saving them.
The job template's timeout is entered in minutes, like the project's and the organization's.

title: Streamed logs no longer add a blank line after each line
audience: Everyone who reads live run or job output.
before: Each streamed output line was followed by an empty line in the raw log and the terminal view.
after: Streamed output keeps each line's own line break and adds none.
action: No action is required.

title: Launchers drain before a restart and verify pinned Python packages
audience: Operators who run launchers with Docker Compose, Helm or docker run, and users of hash-pinned Python requirements.
before: Compose and Kubernetes stopped a launcher after 10 and 30 seconds, before it had drained, so an upgrade or restart with jobs in flight ended running Ansible jobs as lost. The cache populator could not verify pinned Python packages, because the launcher images have no pip, and recorded each attempt as a poisoning. A launcher stopped while starting could leave a firewall container behind.
after: Launchers get time to drain: the Compose files stop them with a 6 minute 30 second grace and the chart gives launcher pods a 390-second termination grace. The populator verifies a pinned package from the package index's published hashes without pip. Firewall containers a stopped launcher left behind are removed.
action: On Docker Compose, replace docker-compose.yml with this release's file. On Helm, nothing is required; raise launcher.terminationGracePeriodSeconds if you raise RUNNER_DRAIN_GRACE. Start docker run launchers with --stop-timeout 390.
details: A failed ansible-playbook with no error output reports its exit code without a trailing colon.

title: Deleting an organization removes its cache records
audience: Platform administrators and organization owners who delete organizations.
before: Deleting an organization removed its cached objects but left the database records that described them.
after: The records go with the organization, and the cache janitor removes records an earlier delete left behind.
action: No action is required.

title: Clearer add-runner dialog and pool settings
audience: Agent pool administrators who add launchers or read pool settings.
before: The add-runner dialog asked for an API key, offered only the in-process command and filled in the app's address, which a split deployment does not serve the API on. Pool rows overlapped at phone width, and pool settings used internal names.
after: The dialog asks for a registration token, offers the container driver, and fills in the API's own address. Pool rows stack at phone width, the pull Secret section says which driver uses it, and the deployment panel shows request limits.
action: No action is required.

title: JSON run errors appear once
audience: Users reading errors from Terraform or OpenTofu JSON output.
before: The same JSON error could appear as two error cards and increase the displayed error count.
after: An error already extracted from a JSON message is shown once. Its complete message and existing plain-text error handling are preserved.
action: No action is required.
details: Fallback extraction remains available for messages that the primary JSON parser does not recognize.

title: GitHub browse links preserve branch and file names
audience: People opening GitHub branch or file links from Stackweaver.
before: A literal # in a GitHub branch or file name became a URL fragment, truncating the path opened by the link.
after: GitHub browse links encode branch and file names while preserving directory separators and literal percent sequences.
action: Update the frontend. No configuration change is required.

title: Registry metadata excludes false submodule entries
audience: People publishing Terraform modules to the private registry.
before: A directory whose name ended in .tf could make its parent appear as a nonempty submodule even when the parent contained no Terraform source files.
after: A .tf directory name alone does not create a submodule in newly published version metadata. Terraform files and genuine nested modules are still detected.
action: Update the API before publishing new module versions. Existing module-version metadata is unchanged.
details: This change does not rewrite existing published versions.

title: Registry resource metadata stays within its module
audience: People publishing Terraform modules with examples or nested directories.
before: Resources declared in example or other nested directories could appear in the selected module version metadata.
after: Newly published version metadata lists resource declarations from the selected module directory, without adding resources from unrelated nested directories.
action: Update the API before publishing new module versions. Existing stored version metadata is unchanged.
details: Resources in nested modules are not added to their parent's declaration list.

title: Ansible image includes ASN.1 decoder security fixes
audience: Operators using the bundled Ansible execution image and its cloud identity dependencies.
before: The bundled ASN.1 decoder had known resource-exhaustion issues when parsing some crafted values.
after: The bundled image includes the maintained decoder fixes for constructed strings, binary real values and schemaless tag tracking.
action: Update the Ansible execution image when this change is published. No configuration change is required. Custom execution images need their own dependency updates.
details: The dependency update preserves existing playbook and inventory configuration.
This entry does not establish publication or absence of other dependency findings.

title: Scheduled and workflow inventory syncs run on a launcher
audience: Teams that sync dynamic inventory sources from schedules or workflows, and operators who set ANSIBLE_SCHEDULER_ENABLED or run more than one API replica.
before: An inventory source schedule, its Run now and a workflow's inventory sync node ran the inventory plugin inside the API, which ships no Ansible, so those syncs failed on production images. With ANSIBLE_SCHEDULER_ENABLED=false a launched workflow did not advance past its first job template node.
after: Every sync of a dynamic source, whatever triggered it, runs on a launcher of the pool its source resolves to. A schedule shows its sync as Queued and then as the sync's outcome, and a workflow sync node finishes when its sync does. ANSIBLE_SCHEDULER_ENABLED=false stops only schedules firing on their cron; workflows, held jobs, schedule outcomes and notifications advance either way, and one API replica at a time does each scheduler tick's work.
action: No configuration change is required. Make sure the pool your inventory sources resolve to has an Ansible launcher online, as it needs for manual syncs.
details: Run now on a schedule of a disabled inventory source answers 409 with the reason.
A running workflow node that recorded no job or sync five minutes after it started fails, and the run follows its failure edges.
A manual sync keeps showing the source's last host count while it runs.

title: Workflow inventory sync nodes name the source they sync
audience: Teams that build Ansible workflows through the API.
before: An inventory_sync workflow node could not be given its inventory source through the API, so such a node failed when its workflow reached it.
after: Create and update a node with the inventory-source relationship. An inventory_sync node requires one, other node types refuse one, and the source must belong to the workflow's organization and to the node's inventory when it names one.
action: Give each existing inventory_sync node its source with a node update.
details: The node read returns the inventory-source relationship.

title: Ansible image includes locking and OAuth dependency security fixes
audience: Operators using the platform Ansible image or custom images based on it or its dependency lockfile.
before: The Ansible image included Filelock and OAuthlib versions affected by known security advisories.
after: The Ansible image includes the maintained upstream fixes in Filelock 4.2.1 and OAuthlib 4.0.1.
action: Update the platform Ansible image to the version listed here. Rebuild derived images with that base, or rebuild lockfile-based images with the updated dependency lockfile.
details: The OAuthlib update validates device-code authorization before issuing a token.
The Filelock update supplies the maintained fixes for the known locking advisories.
